usage: the default greeting to almost anyone you meet
반말, to a close friend, a child, or someone clearly younger
격식체; soldiers, announcers, staff to customers, formal speeches
natural extension when greeting someone you know
examples: 안녕하세요. — 네, 안녕하세요.
Hello. — Yes, hello.
the bare greeting returned with the same words
안녕하세요, 처음 뵙겠습니다.
Hello, nice to meet you (first time).
everyday: chaining a greeting into a first introduction
(가게에 들어가며) 안녕하세요~ 사장님 계세요?
(walking into a shop) Hello~ is the owner in?
real situation: 안녕하세요 doubles as 'excuse me' to get attention
nuance: 안녕하세요 is the all-purpose 존댓말 greeting you use with strangers, coworkers, shopkeepers, teachers — basically any adult you are not close with. It comes from 안녕(安寧) 'peace/well-being' + 하세요, so it literally asks 'are you at peace?', but Koreans hear it simply as 'hello' and it works morning, noon, and night (there is no separate 'good morning/afternoon'). Drop to 반말 안녕 only with close friends, kids, or clear juniors; step up to 안녕하십니까 for formal or service settings. The classic English-speaker mistake is splitting greetings by time of day or adding a literal 'how are you?' every time — in Korean 안녕하세요 alone is the complete, polite hello, and over-asking 어떻게 지내세요? to a stranger sounds oddly probing.

english: Goodbye (said by the person who is leaving).
usage: YOU are leaving; they stay (in their home/shop/office)
반말, leaving a close friend who stays behind
격식체, e.g. leaving a formal office or addressing a superior
goodbye, keep up the good work
warm close to staff/coworkers who remain
examples: 안녕히 계세요. — 네, 안녕히 가세요.
Goodbye. — Yes, goodbye (go well).
the leaver says 계세요, the stayer answers 가세요
(사무실을 나가며) 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. 안녕히 계세요.
(leaving the office) I'll head off first. Goodbye.
everyday: pairs with a polite 'I'll go first' to coworkers
(병원에서 나오며) 선생님, 감사합니다. 안녕히 계세요.
(leaving the clinic) Thank you, doctor. Goodbye.
real situation: patient leaving thanks the doctor who stays
nuance: 안녕히 계세요 is the goodbye YOU say when you are the one leaving and the other person stays — 계시다 is the honorific of 있다 'to be/stay', so you are wishing them 'stay in peace'. Its mirror twin is 안녕히 가세요 (가다 'to go'), said TO the person who is leaving; the moving party decides which verb you pick. Use 반말 잘 있어 with a close friend who stays, and 안녕히 계십시오 in stiff formal settings. The number-one English-speaker error is treating 'goodbye' as one fixed phrase: learners say 안녕히 가세요 as they themselves walk out the door, which literally tells their host to leave their own home. Always ask: am I leaving (계세요) or are they (가세요)?

Spelling it 안녕히 게세요 — the verb is 계시다, so it is 계세요, not 게세요.

usage: 반말, to a close friend or junior who is leaving
격식체; shop/airline/hotel staff to a departing guest
examples: 안녕히 가세요. — 네, 안녕히 계세요.
Goodbye. — Yes, goodbye (stay well).
the stayer says 가세요, the leaver answers 계세요
(손님을 배웅하며) 안녕히 가세요. 또 오세요.
(seeing a customer off) Goodbye. Come again.

(엘리베이터 앞에서) 부장님, 안녕히 가세요. 내일 뵙겠습니다.

nuance: 안녕히 가세요 is the goodbye you say to the person who is LEAVING while you remain — 가다 'to go' + the polite command, so you wish them 'go in peace'. english: Nice to meet you (for the first time). / How do you do.
usage: 격식 존댓말; first introduction to an adult, esp. someone senior
NOT used; 보다 is too plain — the honorific 뵙다 is required here
I think this is the first time we've met
How do you do, I'm Kim Minsu
natural extension straight into your name
examples: 처음 뵙겠습니다. — 네, 처음 뵙겠습니다.
How do you do. — Yes, how do you do.
exchanged once, mutually, at a first meeting
안녕하세요, 처음 뵙겠습니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.
Hello, nice to meet you. I look forward to working with you.
everyday: the standard 3-part first-meeting set
(소개팅/거래처 첫 미팅에서 일어서서 인사하며) 처음 뵙겠습니다. 말씀 많이 들었습니다.
(standing to greet at a blind date / first business meeting) How do you do. I've heard a lot about you.
real situation: pairs with 말씀 많이 들었습니다
nuance: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is the formal, respectful phrase for a FIRST meeting — 처음 'first time' + 뵙겠습니다, where 뵙다 is the humble-honorific form of 보다 'to see/meet', so it literally means 'I will be seeing you for the first time'. You use it to adults, especially seniors, business contacts, or in-laws; among casual peers people often just say 만나서 반가워요 instead. Because 뵙겠습니다 is already deeply humble, there is essentially no 반말 version — with friends you simply wouldn't use this phrase at all. The typical English-speaker mistake is reaching for plain 보다 (처음 보겠습니다), which sounds blunt or even rude, or translating 'nice to meet you' as 만나서 반갑습니다 in a stiff formal setting where 처음 뵙겠습니다 is expected first.

english: Nice to meet you. / Glad to meet you.
usage: 격식 존댓말; introductions at work or with seniors
반말, meeting a friend-of-a-friend your own age or younger
해요체; friendly polite, peers and casual acquaintances
I'm glad to have the chance to meet you
examples: 만나서 반갑습니다. — 저도 반갑습니다.
Nice to meet you. — Nice to meet you too.
reply with 저도 반갑습니다 ('I'm glad too')
민수 씨 친구분이시죠? 만나서 반가워요.
You're Minsu's friend, right? Nice to meet you.
everyday: 해요체 to a peer you've just been introduced to
(명함을 건네며) 안녕하세요, 영업팀 김민수입니다. 만나서 반갑습니다.
(handing over a business card) Hello, I'm Kim Minsu from sales. Nice to meet you.
real situation: card exchange in a business introduction
nuance: 만나서 반갑습니다 means 'I'm glad to meet you' — 만나서 'having met' + 반갑다 'to be glad', so unlike 처음 뵙겠습니다 it focuses on the pleasure of meeting rather than the fact that it's the first time. Pick your ending by closeness: 반갑습니다 (격식, formal/business), 반가워요 (friendly polite peers), 반가워 (반말 with friends/juniors). The common English-speaker error is using only this phrase for every first meeting; in a formal Korean introduction you typically lead with 처음 뵙겠습니다 and then add 만나서 반갑습니다. Also note the reply is 저도 반갑습니다 ('me too'), not a repeated full sentence.

english: I look forward to working with you. / Please treat me kindly. (lit. I ask for your favor.)
usage: I kindly ask for your favor
격식 존댓말; deeply humble, to seniors/clients/new colleagues
take care of me / look out for me
반말, to a close friend or junior
해요체; polite but a touch softer than 드립니다
I'll be relying on you going forward
examples: 잘 부탁드립니다. — 네, 저야말로 잘 부탁드립니다.
I look forward to working with you. — No, the pleasure is mine.
reply with 저야말로 ('it's I who should ask')
오늘부터 함께 일하게 됐습니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.
I'll be working with you starting today. Please treat me kindly.
everyday: a new hire greeting the team
(결혼 상견례에서 고개 숙이며) 부족한 사람이지만 잘 부탁드립니다.

real situation: in-laws meeting; pairs with a bow and 부족한 사람이지만

usage: polite, soft way to ask an adult's name
반말, to a child or close peer/junior
more formal; 성함 is the honorific word for 'name'
natural: offer your own name back
examples: 이름이 어떻게 되세요? — 김민수예요.
What's your name? — I'm Kim Minsu.
the soft polite name question and a simple answer
(첫 수업에서) 학생, 이름이 어떻게 되세요?
(first class) What's your name?
everyday: a teacher asking a new student politely
(전화 접수에서) 네, 예약 도와드릴게요. 성함이 어떻게 되세요?
(phone reception) Sure, I'll help with your booking. May I have your name?

The honorific upgrade swaps 이름 for 성함: 성함이 어떻게 되세요? is what staff, officials, and juniors use toward adults/customers. Drop to 반말 이름이 뭐야? only with children or close juniors. english: Where are you from? / Where did you come from?
usage: honorific 오시다; asking an adult their origin
반말, to a peer or junior
natural variant when asking a foreigner's country
examples: 어디에서 오셨어요? — 미국에서 왔어요.
Where are you from? — I'm from the US.
answer with [place]에서 왔어요
한국말 잘하시네요! 어디에서 오셨어요?
Your Korean is great! Where are you from?
everyday: a common follow-up to a foreigner
(모임에서 자기소개 중) 저는 부산에서 왔어요. 혹시 어디에서 오셨어요?
(self-intro at a gathering) I'm from Busan. Where are you from, by the way?
real situation: trading hometowns, 도시/지역 level
nuance: 어디에서 오셨어요? asks 'where did you come from?' and works for both your home country and your hometown — 오시다 is the honorific of 오다 'to come', and the past tense 오셨- is idiomatic here even though origin is ongoing (Korean frames it as 'where did you set out from'). Note the place particle is 에서 ('from'), not 에. To ask a foreigner's country specifically, 어느 나라에서 오셨어요? is more precise. Drop to 반말 어디에서 왔어? with peers/juniors; go formal with 오셨습니까?. The classic English-speaker errors are using 에 instead of 에서 (에 marks destination, not origin), and dropping the honorific 시 (오셨어요 not 왔어요) when speaking to someone you should respect. The answer keeps 에서: 미국에서 왔어요.

usage: the everyday polite way to ask someone's job

what kind of work do you do?

english: Have you been well? / How have you been?
usage: 해요체; greeting someone you haven't seen in a while
adds honorific 시, toward a senior
been well? nothing's come up, right?

반말, to a close friend or junior
격식체; to a senior or customer

natural variant; swap 하루 for 주말/저녁

반말, to a close friend, sibling, or junior

real situation: 밥 먹었어? as an expression of care/affection
nuance: 밥 먹었어요? literally 'did you eat (rice/a meal)?' is one of Korea's most characteristic greetings — historically food was scarce, so asking whether someone had eaten became a way of showing care, and today it functions much like English 'how are you?' rather than a real question about food. It is NOT an invitation to eat; the expected reply is a quick 네, 먹었어요 / 아직요, then bounce it back. Register ladder: 밥 먹었어? (반말) → 밥 먹었어요? (polite) → 식사하셨어요? (honorific, swapping 밥→식사 and adding 시) → 진지 드셨어요? (to the elderly, with honorific nouns 진지/드시다). The English-speaker mistake is taking it literally and either thinking they're being invited to a meal, or earnestly listing what they ate — Koreans just want the brief ritual reply. Use the 식사하셨어요? / 진지 드셨어요? upgrades for anyone you owe respect; plain 밥 먹었어요? among peers.

Historically food was scarce, so asking whether someone had eaten became a way of showing care — which is why it works as a greeting today.

mistakes: Taking 밥 먹었어요? literally as a dinner invitation — it's a caring greeting like 'how are you?'; just answer 네, 먹었어요 and ask back.
Using 밥 먹었어? (반말) with a senior — upgrade to 식사하셨어요?, or 진지 드셨어요? for an elderly person.
Answering by describing your whole meal — the ritual reply is short (네, 먹었어요 / 아직 안 먹었어요), then return the question.
